title: PRISM: Prompt Refinement via Image-grounded Self-rewarding Mechanism for Text-to-Image Generation

paper.title: PRISM: Prompt Refinement via Image-grounded Self-rewarding Mechanism for Text-to-Image Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Text-to-image generation models can synthesize high-quality images
from natural language descriptions, but their performance remains highly
sensitive to prompt formulation. Existing prompt optimization methods
mainly rely on text-side rewriting, prompt expansion, or external reward
signals, offering limited image-grounded diagnosis and weak support for
learning reusable optimization policies.
In this paper, we propose PRISM , a P rompt R efinement framework via I mage-grounded S elf-rewarding M echanism.
PRISM closes the prompt-image-feedback loop by interpreting generated
images with structured visual diagnosis and scoring them along semantic
consistency, aesthetic quality, and human preference alignment. It first
initializes a unified VLM through multi-task supervised fine-tuning, and
then improves the prompt policy via self-rewarding optimization with a
hybrid ideal-point and Chebyshev reward. Extensive experiments show that
PRISM improves holistic image quality and fine-grained semantic alignment,
while providing interpretable feedback for targeted prompt refinement. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PRISM-FF81

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image (T2I) generation has made remarkable progress in synthesizing high-quality images from natural language descriptions Esser et al. (2024) ; Podell et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2024) . However, its performance remains highly sensitive to prompt formulation, as under-specified prompts often fail to provide the object, attribute, style, and composition details required for controllable and faithful generation Huang et al. (2023) ; Mahajan et al. (2024) . As a result, prompt optimization has become an important technique for improving generation quality Chen et al. (2025) . Figure 1: Motivation of the proposed PRISM framework. Existing prompt optimization methods have explored text-side rewriting, prompt expansion, and reinforcement learning-based prompt adaptation Cao et al. (2023) ; Pavlichenko and Ustalov (2023) ; Yang et al. (2025) . While effective, most of them rely on textual patterns or scalar rewards, providing limited diagnostic guidance on why a generated image succeeds or fails. Recent visual-feedback-based methods incorporate generated images into prompt refinement, but they are often implemented as test-time pipelines with separate critic and rewriter modules, which limits their ability to learn a reusable optimization policy Wu et al. (2025) ; Khan et al. (2025) . Moreover, existing feedback signals usually emphasize isolated objectives, rather than jointly modeling semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and preference alignment within a unified framework Zhang et al. (2024) . As illustrated in Fig. 1 , these limitations suggest that prompt optimization should be guided by structured visual feedback derived from what the generated image actually shows. Motivated by this observation, we propose PRISM , a Prompt Refinement framework via Image-grounded Self-rewarding Mechanism for T2I prompt optimization. Instead of learning prompt rewriting solely from text pairs, our method directly interprets generated images through structured visual diagnosis and uses the feedback to guide prompt optimization. Specifically, we train a Vision-Language Model (VLM) to assess generated images along three complementary dimensions: semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and human preference alignment. The predicted diagnostic feedback and dimension-specific scores are then used for both prompt revision and reward computation. We initialize the VLM through multi-task supervised fine-tuning for joint prompt rewriting and visual feedback assessment, and further optimize the prompt policy via self-rewarding learning using Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) Zheng et al. (2025) . A hybrid ideal-point and Chebyshev reward encourages the optimized prompts to approach the ideal visual feedback scores while penalizing weak dimensions, leading to more balanced improvements. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: • PRISM framework. We propose a unified multimodal framework that learns a reusable prompt optimization policy by integrating visual feedback assessment and prompt rewriting. • A diagnosis-guided reward mechanism. We introduce a multi-dimensional reward mechanism based on structured visual diagnosis, where semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and human preference alignment are jointly considered through a hybrid ideal-point and Chebyshev objective. • Comprehensive empirical validation. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of PRISM in prompt optimization and targeted feedback-guided refinement.

sections.heading: 2.1 Text-to-Image generation
sections.text: T2I generation aims to synthesize visually realistic and semantically aligned images from natural language descriptions. Early studies explored GAN-based text-conditioned generation Reed et al. (2016) ; Zhang et al. (2017) ; Xu et al. (2018) , while autoregressive models further formulated image synthesis as sequence modeling over visual tokens Ramesh et al. (2021) ; Ding et al. (2021) . More recently, diffusion models have become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity T2I generation Ho et al. (2020) ; Dhariwal and Nichol (2021) . Representative systems such as GLIDE Nichol et al. (2021) , Imagen Saharia et al. (2022) , Latent Diffusion Models Rombach et al. (2022) , SDXL Podell et al. (2024) , and Stable Diffusion 3 Esser et al. (2024) have substantially improved photorealism, image-text alignment, efficiency, and high-resolution synthesis. Despite these advances, T2I models remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation. Well-designed prompts are often required to specify objects, attributes, relations, style, and composition, making prompt engineering and automatic prompt optimization important directions for controllable and preference-aligned generation.

sections.heading: 2.2 Prompt Engineering
sections.text: Prompt engineering aims to improve the controllability, fidelity, and visual quality of T2I generation by refining input prompts. For example, BestPrompt searches effective prompt keywords with genetic algorithms Pavlichenko and Ustalov (2023) , and PEZ optimizes discrete hard prompts via gradient-based search Wen et al. (2023) . Promptist learns to adapt user inputs into model-preferred prompts using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning Hao et al. (2023) , while BeautifulPrompt further leverages visual AI feedback Cao et al. (2023) . More recently, self-rewarding VLMs have been explored to unify prompt rewriting and image evaluation within a single model Yang et al. (2025) . Although these methods improve prompt quality, they provide limited image-grounded diagnosis of generation failures. Beyond text-side optimization, recent methods incorporate generated images or external evaluators into prompt refinement. PromptMagician supports interactive prompt exploration by retrieving similar prompt-image pairs and recommending important keywords Feng et al. (2023) . OPT2I iteratively revises prompts with an LLM to maximize prompt-image consistency Mañas et al. (2024) , while T2I-Copilot Chen et al. (2025) and PromptSculptor Xiang et al. (2025) employ multi-agent systems for evaluator-guided refinement. TIR performs closed-loop test-time refinement by using an MLLM to check prompt-image alignment and update prompts with history-aware feedback Khan et al. (2025) . VisualPrompter further decomposes prompts into atomic semantic concepts with Davidsonian Scene Graphs Cho et al. (2024) and uses visual feedback to identify missing concepts for target-specific optimization Wu et al. (2025) . These feedback-aware methods show the value of generated images for prompt refinement, but they are often constrained by fragmented feedback objectives, reliance on external or test-time evaluators, and limited ability to transform structured visual feedback into a reusable self-optimizing prompt policy.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: In this section, we introduce PRISM for image-grounded self-rewarding prompt refinement. The overall framework is shown in Fig. 2 . We formulate prompt optimization as a closed-loop process that connects the user prompt, prompt optimizer, T2I generator, and generated image. Based on structured visual feedback, we introduce a two-stage training procedure consisting of supervised initialization and self-rewarding prompt optimization. Figure 2: Overview of the proposed PRISM framework. Stage I performs multi-task supervised initialization to equip the VLM with prompt rewriting and visual feedback assessment abilities. Stage II optimizes the prompt policy through self-rewarding learning, where candidate prompts are rendered by a frozen T2I generator, evaluated with structured visual feedback, and updated using hybrid reward aggregation. The bottom row illustrates an inference example of feedback-guided prompt refinement.

sections.heading: 3.2 Visual Feedback Construction
sections.text: As defined in Equation ( 2 ), visual feedback ℱ \mathcal{F} contains both textual diagnosis and numerical scores along three dimensions: semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and preference alignment. Semantic consistency measures whether the generated image preserves the original user intent, including objects, attributes, actions, counting, spatial relations, and interactions. Aesthetic quality evaluates visual appeal beyond semantic correctness, such as composition, lighting, color harmony, clarity, details, and artifacts. Preference alignment captures holistic user-oriented judgments, including naturalness, coherence, style appropriateness, attractiveness, and overall satisfaction. Details are provided in the Appendix A.4 .

I_{i}=G(\hat{x}_{i}). sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Settings
sections.text: We adopt Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct Bai et al. (2025) as the backbone VLM. Stable Diffusion 3.5 medium 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-medium is used as the primary target T2I generator with 28 denoising steps, while additional results on FLUX.2-klein 2 2 2 https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.2-klein-4B are reported in Appendix C to evaluate cross-generator generalization. Supervised fine-tuning. We train the VLM with AdamW Loshchilov and Hutter (2017) using β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 , a batch size of 32, and weight decay of 0.1. The learning rate is initialized to 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} and scheduled with linear warm-up followed by cosine decay. For the multi-task SFT objective, we set the task loss weights to λ rew : λ fb : λ score : λ fgr = 1 : 1 : 1 : 2 \lambda_{\mathrm{rew}}:\lambda_{\mathrm{fb}}:\lambda_{\mathrm{score}}:\lambda_{\mathrm{fgr}}=1:1:1:2 emphasizing feedback-guided prompt rewriting. Self-rewarding optimization. For each input prompt, the policy samples K = 8 K=8 candidate prompts with temperature T = 0.9 T=0.9 and top- p = 0.9 p=0.9 . We set the sequence-level clipping threshold to ϵ c = 0.2 \epsilon_{c}=0.2 and the KL coefficient to β = 0.3 \beta=0.3 , using the SFT model as the reference policy π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} . The scalar reward follows the hybrid aggregation strategy in Section 3.4 , with 𝐰 = [ 0.5 , 0.25 , 0.25 ] \mathbf{w}=[0.5,0.25,0.25] to emphasize semantic consistency. Each visual assessment is repeated three times and averaged for stability. We perform two self-rewarding iterations. During training and evaluation, all T2I generators are frozen. All methods are evaluated under the same generation settings for fair comparison. All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A800 80G GPUs.

sections.heading: 4.2 Benchmarks and Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: We evaluate PRISM on two types of benchmarks. For general prompt optimization, we use the 2k BeautifulPrompt test prompts Cao et al. (2023) and report CLIPScore Hessel et al. (2021) , Aesthetic Score Podell et al. (2024) , ImageReward Xu et al. (2023) , PickScore Kirstain et al. (2023) , and HPSv2 Wu et al. (2023) to measure image-text alignment, visual quality, and human preference. For fine-grained semantic alignment, we evaluate on T2I-CompBench Huang et al. (2023) and TIFA Hu et al. (2023) . T2I-CompBench assesses compositional generation over attributes, relations, and complex prompts, while TIFA measures prompt-image faithfulness via automatically generated visual questions. For all benchmarks, metrics are computed with respect to the original user prompt rather than the optimized prompt, ensuring that the evaluation reflects preservation and enhancement of the original user intent.

Starting from the original prompt, we perform multiple refinement rounds by feeding the generated image and its visual feedback back into the model. As shown in Fig. 3 , the second refinement round brings additional improvements, especially for samples with low first-pass scores. This suggests that PRISM can act as a feedback-aware prompt optimizer rather than a one-shot prompt enhancer. Effect of reward aggregation. Table 4 compares different reward aggregation strategies. The hybrid reward achieves the best performance across all metrics. Compared with the weighted-sum reward, the hybrid strategy further improves TIFA by 3.3 points while maintaining slightly better aesthetic and preference scores. Although the ideal-point and Chebyshev rewards improve semantic faithfulness over the weighted-sum baseline, they show weaker aesthetic or preference performance when used alone. These results indicate that combining overall closeness to the ideal feedback profile with worst-dimension penalty leads to more balanced prompt optimization. sections.heading: 4.5 Qualitative Analysis
sections.text: Fig. 4 presents representative examples of the visual-feedback-guided prompt refinement process in PRISM. The model identifies concrete generation issues, such as missing objects, weak spatial relations, and style mismatch, and revises the prompt accordingly. These examples demonstrate that structured visual feedback provides interpretable correction cues for targeted prompt refinement.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we propose PRISM, a Prompt Refinement framework via Image-grounded Self-rewarding Mechanism for text-to-image prompt optimization. PRISM uses structured visual diagnosis to guide prompt rewriting and reward computation across semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and preference alignment. Through multi-task supervised initialization and self-rewarding policy optimization, the VLM learns to jointly perform prompt rewriting and visual feedback assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PRISM improves holistic image quality and fine-grained semantic alignment, while providing interpretable feedback for targeted prompt refinement.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Although PRISM demonstrates strong effectiveness, several aspects remain open for future work. First, the current feedback design focuses on semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and preference alignment; extending it to more fine-grained or domain-specific criteria could further improve controllability. Second, iterative feedback refinement is evaluated with a limited number of rounds to maintain inference efficiency, while adaptive stopping strategies may provide a better trade-off between quality and cost.

sections.heading: A.3.1 Candidate pool construction
sections.text: We construct feedback-oriented data from publicly available and license-permissive AI-generated image resources. Rather than processing full-scale community datasets, we first sample a tractable candidate pool 𝒰 T2I \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{T2I}} with C C image-text pairs. In our implementation, we set C = 50,000 C=50{,}000 and perform all metric computation and filtering only within this sampled pool. The pool can be instantiated from open community T2I resources, including DiffusionDB, JourneyDB, and Pick-a-Pic, depending on data availability and experimental needs. Each candidate sample is represented as ( x ^ i , I i + ) (\hat{x}_{i},I_{i}^{+}) , where x ^ i \hat{x}_{i} is a community-written prompt and I i + I_{i}^{+} is its associated generated image. Since community prompts often contain rich visual details and generation-oriented expressions, we treat x ^ i \hat{x}_{i} as a model-preferred prompt. For each candidate pair, we compute three quality indicators: a i a_{i} for aesthetic quality, p i p_{i} for preference alignment, and c i c_{i} for image-text alignment. After min–max normalization within 𝒰 T2I \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{T2I}} , we compute the unified quality score in Equation( ( 22 )) and retain the top N 2 = 5,000 N_{2}=5{,}000 high-quality pairs. The retained high-quality pool is denoted as 𝒟 high = { ( x ^ i , I i + ) } i = 1 N 2 \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{high}}=\{(\hat{x}_{i},I_{i}^{+})\}_{i=1}^{N_{2}} . This pool serves as the source for constructing paired prompts ( x i , x ^ i ) (x_{i},\hat{x}_{i}) and their feedback-oriented supervision.

sections.heading: A.3.2 Controlled prompt simplification
sections.text: For each high-quality prompt x ^ i \hat{x}_{i} , we apply a stochastic simplification operator 𝒯 \mathcal{T} to construct an under-specified counterpart x i = 𝒯 ⁡ ( x ^ i ) x_{i}=\mathcal{T}(\hat{x}_{i}) . The goal is not to introduce semantic errors, but to preserve the core intent while removing details that are commonly missing in user-provided prompts. This yields paired prompts ( x i , x ^ i ) (x_{i},\hat{x}_{i}) with explicit optimization gaps. The simplification process follows four primary strategies: • Summarization and abstraction ( 30 % 30\% ). We compress a long prompt into a short sentence or tag chain, with target length ratio r ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0.25 , 0.50 ) r\sim\mathcal{U}(0.25,0.50) . Fine-grained nouns may be replaced by more generic hypernyms, while the main entity and action are retained. For example, a Victorian gothic cathedral, dramatic backlight, intricate stone texture is simplified to an old cathedral with dramatic light . • Removal of style and quality modifiers ( 25 % 25\% ). We remove common style, quality, and rendering modifiers, such as masterpiece, best quality, ultra-detailed, 8k, RAW photo, cinematic lighting, octane render, artstation, unreal engine, sharp focus . Specifically, we randomly delete 60 % ∼ 100 % 60\%\!\sim\!100\% of matched modifiers. For example, masterpiece, ultra detailed, 8k, cinematic lighting, 1 girl is reduced to 1 girl . • Weakening attributes, relations, scenes, and composition ( 30 % 30\% ). We decompose x ^ i \hat{x}_{i} into atomic semantic units and remove ∼ 3 1\!\sim\!3 non-core atoms, preferably attributes, relations, scene details, and composition descriptions. This includes removing color, material, texture, clothing, spatial relations, exact counts, camera views, and framing details. For example, three red apples on the left side of a wooden table, close-up shot is simplified to apples on a table . • Omission of secondary entities ( 15 % 15\% ). When a prompt contains multiple entities, background objects, or auxiliary events, we keep the main entity and at most one supporting entity, while removing peripheral clauses and minor interactions. For example, a boy reading near a window, with a cat on the sofa and plants in the background is simplified to a boy reading near a window . To improve degradation diversity, we additionally apply one secondary micro-edit with probability 0.35 0.35 . During simplification, we enforce three constraints: at least one main entity is preserved, the token retention ratio satisfies r ∈ [ 0.25 , 0.70 ] r\in[0.25,0.70] , and the degraded prompt is non-empty. For each paired prompt sample ( x i , x ^ i ) (x_{i},\hat{x}_{i}) , we associate images with prompts p ∈ { x i , x ^ i } p\in\{x_{i},\hat{x}_{i}\} . Specifically, I i I_{i} is generated by the frozen target T2I generator G G , i.e., I i = G ⁡ ( x i ) I_{i}=G(x_{i}) . For the optimized prompt x ^ i \hat{x}_{i} , we reuse the original community image I i + I_{i}^{+} . This produces intermediate prompt-image samples of the form { x i , I i , x ^ i , I i + } \{x_{i},I_{i},\hat{x}_{i},I_{i}^{+}\} . These samples are then organized into the feedback assessment, score-only calibration, and feedback-guided rewriting datasets described below.

sections.text: The constructed samples are organized into four supervision formats, consistent with the main paper. Table 5 summarizes the training datasets.

sections.heading: Prompt rewriting data.
sections.text: The first type is prompt rewriting data: 𝒟 rew = { ( x , x ^ ∗ ) } . \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rew}}=\{(x,\hat{x}^{*})\}. (27) We use a curated 10 10 k-sample subset of BeautifulPrompt. This dataset teaches the prompt optimizer π θ \pi_{\theta} to transform simple or under-specified user prompts into more detailed and model-preferred prompts.

sections.heading: Visual feedback assessment data.
sections.text: The second type is visual feedback assessment data: 𝒟 fb = { ( p , I p , ℱ p ∗ ) } . \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fb}}=\{(p,I_{p},\mathcal{F}^{*}_{p})\}. (28) Here, p ∈ { x i , x ^ i } p\in\{x_{i},\hat{x}_{i}\} , I p I_{p} is the generated or reused image associated with prompt p p , and ℱ p ∗ \mathcal{F}^{*}_{p} contains structured diagnostic feedback and scores over semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and preference alignment. This dataset initializes the model’s ability to assess generated images and produce interpretable feedback.

sections.heading: Score-only calibration data.
sections.text: To stabilize numerical scoring, we additionally construct score-only calibration data: 𝒟 score = { ( p , I p , 𝐫 p ∗ ) } . \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{score}}=\{(p,I_{p},\mathbf{r}^{*}_{p})\}. (29) This subset removes long-form diagnostic text and retains only the score vector 𝐫 p ∗ = [ r p , sem ∗ , r p , aes ∗ , r p , pref ∗ ] \mathbf{r}^{*}_{p}=[r^{*}_{p,\mathrm{sem}},r^{*}_{p,\mathrm{aes}},r^{*}_{p,\mathrm{pref}}] . sections.heading: Feedback-guided prompt rewriting data.
sections.text: The final instruction type is feedback-guided prompt rewriting data: 𝒟 fgr = { ( x i , I i , ℱ x i ∗ , x ^ i ) } . \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fgr}}=\{(x_{i},I_{i},\mathcal{F}^{*}_{x_{i}},\hat{x}_{i})\}. (30) Unlike 𝒟 fb \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fb}} , this task explicitly connects visual diagnosis with prompt revision. Given an under-specified prompt x i x_{i} , its generated image I i = G ⁡ ( x i ) I_{i}=G(x_{i}) , and its visual feedback ℱ x i ∗ \mathcal{F}^{*}_{x_{i}} , the model is trained to revise the prompt toward the optimized counterpart x ^ i \hat{x}_{i} . This encourages the model to use visual feedback as explicit correction cues rather than treating image assessment and prompt rewriting as isolated tasks.

sections.heading: Appendix B Training Data Prompt Templates
sections.text: We provide the prompt templates used to construct the four types of training data. Each template is written in an instruction-style format, matching the actual input-output structure used during data generation. Prompt Rewriting Template for 𝒟 rew \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rew}} Please rewrite the following T2I prompt into a higher-quality prompt. The rewritten prompt should: • preserve the original user intent; • improve visual descriptiveness and clarity; • add appropriate details about attributes, scene, composition, style, and image quality; • avoid introducing objects or meanings that are inconsistent with the original prompt; • be suitable for T2I generation. Original prompt: {x} Output format: Optimized prompt: <Your rewritten prompt > Visual Feedback Template for 𝒟 fb \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fb}} [IMAGE] Please evaluate the generated image according to the given prompt. Prompt: {p} Task. Assess the image from three dimensions: semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and preference alignment. For each dimension, provide a discrete score from 1 to 10 and a concise image-grounded explanation. The scoring should follow the scoring reference box provided below in Appendix B . The three dimensions should be judged independently. Output format: Semantic consistency score: <score from 1 to 10 > Semantic consistency feedback: <concise explanation > Aesthetic quality score: <score from 1 to 10 > Aesthetic quality feedback: <concise explanation > Preference alignment score: <score from 1 to 10 > Preference alignment feedback: <concise explanation > Visual Score Template for 𝒟 score \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{score}} [IMAGE] Please score the generated image according to the given prompt. Prompt: {p} Task. Assign three independent scores from 1 to 10 for semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and preference alignment, following the scoring reference box provided below in Appendix B . Only output the numerical scores without additional explanations. Output format: Semantic consistency score: <score from 1 to 10 > Aesthetic quality score: <score from 1 to 10 > Preference alignment score: <score from 1 to 10 > Feedback-Guided Refinement Template for 𝒟 fgr \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fgr}} [IMAGE] Please refine the original T2I prompt according to the generated image and the visual feedback. Original prompt: {x} Visual feedback: { ℱ x ∗ \mathcal{F}^{*}_{x} } Task: Rewrite the original prompt to improve the next generated image. The refined prompt should: • preserve the original user intent; • correct semantic omissions, weak attribute binding, and relationship-level inconsistencies mentioned in the feedback; • improve aesthetic quality by adding appropriate visual details about composition, lighting, style, and image quality; • improve preference alignment while avoiding unnecessary or inconsistent content; • remain concise and suitable for T2I generation. Output format: Refined prompt: <Your feedback-guided optimized prompt > For 𝒟 fb \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fb}} and 𝒟 score \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{score}} , all visual scores are assigned according to a shared 1–10 scoring rubric. This shared reference ensures consistent criteria between feedback annotation and reward score generation. The detailed scoring rubric is provided below. Scoring Reference for Visual Evaluation All visual scores are assigned on a discrete scale from 1 to 10, where higher scores indicate better quality. The three dimensions are evaluated independently. Semantic consistency. Score 1: almost unrelated to the prompt. Score 2: only a few prompt elements are captured. Score 3: some relevant content is present but with clear semantic errors. Score 4: the main intent is partially followed, with several missing or inconsistent details. Score 5: the main idea is captured, but fine-grained attributes or relations are weak. Score 6: most major elements are correct, with remaining detail-level errors. Score 7: generally consistent with minor omissions. Score 8: accurately reflects most objects, attributes, relations, and scene details. Score 9: highly faithful with negligible imperfections. Score 10: fully matches the prompt, including objects, attributes, relations, actions, and scene details. Aesthetic quality. Score 1: severe aesthetic flaws and poor visual balance. Score 2: major issues in composition, color, lighting, or clarity. Score 3: limited visual appeal with obvious flaws. Score 4: understandable but weak in composition or harmony. Score 5: acceptable but generic or noticeably improvable. Score 6: moderately appealing but lacking refinement. Score 7: good composition, color, lighting, and overall appeal. Score 8: visually strong, coherent, and well balanced. Score 9: excellent harmony, creativity, and visual impact. Score 10: outstanding aesthetic quality with exceptional composition, balance, and creativity. Preference alignment. Score 1: highly unlikely to satisfy human preference. Score 2: low appeal with major issues in naturalness, coherence, or style. Score 3: partially acceptable but with obvious preference-related flaws. Score 4: limited appeal and possibly awkward or inconsistent. Score 5: acceptable but not especially attractive or satisfying. Score 6: moderately preferred with reasonable coherence and appeal. Score 7: likely to be preferred by users. Score 8: strongly preferred, with appealing content and coherent style. Score 9: highly preferred with strong attractiveness and satisfaction. Score 10: exceptionally satisfying and highly aligned with human preference.

Existing prompt optimization methods mainly rely on text-side rewriting, prompt expansion, or external reward signals, offering limited image-grounded diagnosis and weak support for learning reusable optimization policies. In this paper, we propose PRISM , a P rompt R efinement framework via I mage-grounded S elf-rewarding M echanism. PRISM closes the prompt-image-feedback loop by interpreting generated images with structured visual diagnosis and scoring them along semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and human preference alignment. It first initializes a unified VLM through multi-task supervised fine-tuning, and then improves the prompt policy via self-rewarding optimization with a hybrid ideal-point and Chebyshev reward. Extensive experiments show that PRISM improves holistic image quality and fine-grained semantic alignment, while providing interpretable feedback for targeted prompt refinement. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PRISM-FF81 1 Introduction Text-to-image (T2I) generation has made remarkable progress in synthesizing high-quality images from natural language descriptions Esser et al. (2024) ; Podell et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2024) . However, its performance remains highly sensitive to prompt formulation, as under-specified prompts often fail to provide the object, attribute, style, and composition details required for controllable and faithful generation Huang et al. (2023) ; Mahajan et al. (2024) . As a result, prompt optimization has become an important technique for improving generation quality Chen et al. (2025) . Figure 1: Motivation of the proposed PRISM framework. Existing prompt optimization methods have explored text-side rewriting, prompt expansion, and reinforcement learning-based prompt adaptation Cao et al. (2023) ; Pavlichenko and Ustalov (2023) ; Yang et al. (2025) . While effective, most of them rely on textual patterns or scalar rewards, providing limited diagnostic guidance on why a generated image succeeds or fails. Recent visual-feedback-based methods incorporate generated images into prompt refinement, but they are often implemented as test-time pipelines with separate critic and rewriter modules, which limits their ability to learn a reusable optimization policy Wu et al. (2025) ; Khan et al. (2025) . Moreover, existing feedback signals usually emphasize isolated objectives, rather than jointly modeling semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and preference alignment within a unified framework Zhang et al. (2024) . As illustrated in Fig. 1 , these limitations suggest that prompt optimization should be guided by structured visual feedback derived from what the generated image actually shows. Motivated by this observation, we propose PRISM , a Prompt Refinement framework via Image-grounded Self-rewarding Mechanism for T2I prompt optimization. Instead of learning prompt rewriting solely from text pairs, our method directly interprets generated images through structured visual diagnosis and uses the feedback to guide prompt optimization. Specifically, we train a Vision-Language Model (VLM) to assess generated images along three complementary dimensions: semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and human preference alignment. The predicted diagnostic feedback and dimension-specific scores are then used for both prompt revision and reward computation. We initialize the VLM through multi-task supervised fine-tuning for joint prompt rewriting and visual feedback assessment, and further optimize the prompt policy via self-rewarding learning using Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) Zheng et al. (2025) . A hybrid ideal-point and Chebyshev reward encourages the optimized prompts to approach the ideal visual feedback scores while penalizing weak dimensions, leading to more balanced improvements. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: • PRISM framework. We propose a unified multimodal framework that learns a reusable prompt optimization policy by integrating visual feedback assessment and prompt rewriting. • A diagnosis-guided reward mechanism. We introduce a multi-dimensional reward mechanism based on structured visual diagnosis, where semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and human preference alignment are jointly considered through a hybrid ideal-point and Chebyshev objective. • Comprehensive empirical validation. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of PRISM in prompt optimization and targeted feedback-guided refinement. 2 Related Work 2.1 Text-to-Image generation T2I generation aims to synthesize visually realistic and semantically aligned images from natural language descriptions. Early studies explored GAN-based text-conditioned generation Reed et al. (2016) ; Zhang et al. (2017) ; Xu et al. (2018) , while autoregressive models further formulated image synthesis as sequence modeling over visual tokens Ramesh et al. (2021) ; Ding et al. (2021) . More recently, diffusion models have become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity T2I generation Ho et al. (2020) ; Dhariwal and Nichol (2021) . Representative systems such as GLIDE Nichol et al. (2021) , Imagen Saharia et al. (2022) , Latent Diffusion Models Rombach et al. (2022) , SDXL Podell et al. (2024) , and Stable Diffusion 3 Esser et al. (2024) have substantially improved photorealism, image-text alignment, efficiency, and high-resolution synthesis. Despite these advances, T2I models remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation. Well-designed prompts are often required to specify objects, attributes, relations, style, and composition, making prompt engineering and automatic prompt optimization important directions for controllable and preference-aligned generation. 2.2 Prompt Engineering Prompt engineering aims to improve the controllability, fidelity, and visual quality of T2I generation by refining input prompts. For example, BestPrompt searches effective prompt keywords with genetic algorithms Pavlichenko and Ustalov (2023) , and PEZ optimizes discrete hard prompts via gradient-based search Wen et al. (2023) . Promptist learns to adapt user inputs into model-preferred prompts using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning Hao et al. (2023) , while BeautifulPrompt further leverages visual AI feedback Cao et al. (2023) . More recently, self-rewarding VLMs have been explored to unify prompt rewriting and image evaluation within a single model Yang et al. (2025) . Although these methods improve prompt quality, they provide limited image-grounded diagnosis of generation failures. Beyond text-side optimization, recent methods incorporate generated images or external evaluators into prompt refinement. PromptMagician supports interactive prompt exploration by retrieving similar prompt-image pairs and recommending important keywords Feng et al. (2023) . OPT2I iteratively revises prompts with an LLM to maximize prompt-image consistency Mañas et al. (2024) , while T2I-Copilot Chen et al. (2025) and PromptSculptor Xiang et al. (2025) employ multi-agent systems for evaluator-guided refinement. TIR performs closed-loop test-time refinement by using an MLLM to check prompt-image alignment and update prompts with history-aware feedback Khan et al. (2025) . VisualPrompter further decomposes prompts into atomic semantic concepts with Davidsonian Scene Graphs Cho et al. (2024) and uses visual feedback to identify missing concepts for target-specific optimization Wu et al. (2025) . These feedback-aware methods show the value of generated images for prompt refinement, but they are often constrained by fragmented feedback objectives, reliance on external or test-time evaluators, and limited ability to transform structured visual feedback into a reusable self-optimizing prompt policy. 3 Methodology In this section, we introduce PRISM for image-grounded self-rewarding prompt refinement. The overall framework is shown in Fig. 2 . We formulate prompt optimization as a closed-loop process that connects the user prompt, prompt optimizer, T2I generator, and generated image. Based on structured visual feedback, we introduce a two-stage training procedure consisting of supervised initialization and self-rewarding prompt optimization. Figure 2: Overview of the proposed PRISM framework. Stage I performs multi-task supervised initialization to equip the VLM with prompt rewriting and visual feedback assessment abilities. Stage II optimizes the prompt policy through self-rewarding learning, where candidate prompts are rendered by a frozen T2I generator, evaluated with structured visual feedback, and updated using hybrid reward aggregation. (5) 3.2 Visual Feedback Construction As defined in Equation ( 2 ), visual feedback ℱ \mathcal{F} contains both textual diagnosis and numerical scores along three dimensions: semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and preference alignment. Semantic consistency measures whether the generated image preserves the original user intent, including objects, attributes, actions, counting, spatial relations, and interactions. Aesthetic quality evaluates visual appeal beyond semantic correctness, such as composition, lighting, color harmony, clarity, details, and artifacts. Preference alignment captures holistic user-oriented judgments, including naturalness, coherence, style appropriateness, attractiveness, and overall satisfaction. Details are provided in the Appendix A.4 . 3.3 Supervised Initialization for Prompt Rewriting and Visual Feedback Assessment Before self-rewarding optimization, the VLM is initialized with two core abilities: prompt rewriting and structured visual feedback assessment. We train a single VLM under a multi-task supervised objective, enabling it to act as both the prompt optimizer and the feedback provider in the subsequent optimization stage. Training data construction. We construct the supervised dataset from four instruction types: 𝒟 sup = 𝒟 rew ∪ 𝒟 fb ∪ 𝒟 score ∪ 𝒟 fgr . \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sup}}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rew}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fb}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{score}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fgr}}. (6) The prompt rewriting set is defined as 𝒟 rew = { ( x , x ^ ∗ ) } , \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{rew}}=\{(x,\hat{x}^{*})\}, (7) where x x is the user prompt and x ^ ∗ \hat{x}^{*} is the reference optimized prompt. The visual feedback assessment set is defined as 𝒟 fb = { ( p , I p , ℱ p ∗ ) } , p ∈ { x , x ^ ∗ } , I p = G ⁡ ( p ) , \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fb}}=\{(p,I_{p},\mathcal{F}^{*}_{p})\},\ p\in\{x,\hat{x}^{*}\},\ I_{p}=G(p), (8) where ℱ p ∗ \mathcal{F}^{*}_{p} contains reference diagnostic feedback and dimension-specific scores. To calibrate numerical judgment, we further construct a score-only subset 𝒟 score = { ( p , I p , 𝐫 p ∗ ) } , \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{score}}=\{(p,I_{p},\mathbf{r}^{*}_{p})\}, (9) where 𝐫 p ∗ = [ r sem ∗ , r aes ∗ , r pref ∗ ] \mathbf{r}^{*}_{p}=[r^{*}_{\mathrm{sem}},r^{*}_{\mathrm{aes}},r^{*}_{\mathrm{pref}}] . Finally, the feedback guided rewriting set is defined as 𝒟 fgr = { ( x , I x , ℱ x ∗ , x ^ ∗ ) } , \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{fgr}}=\{(x,I_{x},\mathcal{F}^{*}_{x},\hat{x}^{*})\}, (10) which trains the model to revise under-specified prompts using explicit visual feedback. Detailed data construction procedures and instruction templates are provided in Appendix A . Multi-task supervised fine-tuning. All training samples are converted into instruction-following formats and can be viewed in the Appendix B . Let 𝒯 = { rew , fb , score , fgr } \mathcal{T}=\{\mathrm{rew},\mathrm{fb},\mathrm{score},\mathrm{fgr}\} denote the set of supervised tasks, corresponding to prompt rewriting, visual feedback assessment, score-only calibration, and feedback-guided prompt rewriting, respectively. For each task t ∈ 𝒯 t\in\mathcal{T} , we denote the instruction input as u u and the target response as y y . The model is optimized with a response-only autoregressive objective: ℒ SFT = − ∑ t ∈ 𝒯 λ t 𝔼 ( u , y ) ∼ 𝒟 t [ ∑ j = 1 | y | log π θ ( y j ∣ u , y < j ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=-\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{t}\mathbb{E}_{(u,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{|y|}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{j}\mid u,y_{<j})\right], (11) where λ t \lambda_{t} controls the contribution of task t t , and 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} denotes its corresponding training set. Task-specific instructions are used to specify the expected output format, including optimized prompts, diagnostic feedback with scores, score-only responses, and feedback-guided revised prompts. This multi-task initialization enables the same VLM to perform both prompt rewriting and visual feedback assessment, providing the starting policy for self-rewarding optimization. 3.4 Self-Rewarding Prompt Optimization After supervised initialization, the VLM is further optimized through self-rewarding training. In each iteration, the model acts as a prompt policy to generate candidate prompts and as a visual judge to provide reward signals. These examples demonstrate that structured visual feedback provides interpretable correction cues for targeted prompt refinement. 5 Conclusion In this paper, we propose PRISM, a Prompt Refinement framework via Image-grounded Self-rewarding Mechanism for text-to-image prompt optimization. PRISM uses structured visual diagnosis to guide prompt rewriting and reward computation across semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and preference alignment. Through multi-task supervised initialization and self-rewarding policy optimization, the VLM learns to jointly perform prompt rewriting and visual feedback assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PRISM improves holistic image quality and fine-grained semantic alignment, while providing interpretable feedback for targeted prompt refinement. Limitations Although PRISM demonstrates strong effectiveness, several aspects remain open for future work. First, the current feedback design focuses on semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and preference alignment; extending it to more fine-grained or domain-specific criteria could further improve controllability. Second, iterative feedback refinement is evaluated with a limited number of rounds to maintain inference efficiency, while adaptive stopping strategies may provide a better trade-off between quality and cost.
